claim: The last common ancestor of mice and humans existed around 80 million years ago.
source: The last common ancestor of mice and humans existed around 80 million years ago, sufficient time for divergence in signal-dependent gene regulation (Villar et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Villar et al., 2014.

claim: 80 million years is sufficient time for divergence in signal-dependent gene regulation between mice and humans.
source: The last common ancestor of mice and humans existed around 80 million years ago, sufficient time for divergence in signal-dependent gene regulation (Villar et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Villar et al., 2014.

claim: Activity-dependent transcriptional programs are triggered via Ca2+ influx through ligand- and/or voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
source: A fundamental transcriptional program of this sort is that elicited in neurons by electrical activity, triggered via Ca2+ influx through ligand- and/or voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and activating genes containing Ca2+-responsive transcription factor binding sites in their promoters (Sheng and Greenberg, 1990; Morgan and Curran, 1991; West et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sheng and Greenberg, 1990; Morgan and Curran, 1991; West et al., 2001.

claim: Activity-dependent transcriptional programs activate genes containing Ca2+-responsive transcription factor binding sites in their promoters.
source: A fundamental transcriptional program of this sort is that elicited in neurons by electrical activity, triggered via Ca2+ influx through ligand- and/or voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and activating genes containing Ca2+-responsive transcription factor binding sites in their promoters (Sheng and Greenberg, 1990; Morgan and Curran, 1991; West et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sheng and Greenberg, 1990; Morgan and Curran, 1991; West et al., 2001.

claim: Changes in gene expression are critical to a neuron's functional response to electrical activity in development and maturity.
source: These changes in gene expression are critical to a neuron's functional response to electrical activity in development and maturity (Konur and Ghosh, 2005; West and Greenberg, 2011; Bell and Hardingham, 2011), and are totally distinct from the toxic sequelae of excitotoxic Ca2+ influx (Hardingham and Bading, 2010; Wyllie et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Konur and Ghosh, 2005; West and Greenberg, 2011; Bell and Hardingham, 2011.

claim: Activity-dependent gene expression changes are totally distinct from the toxic sequelae of excitotoxic Ca2+ influx.
source: These changes in gene expression are critical to a neuron's functional response to electrical activity in development and maturity (Konur and Ghosh, 2005; West and Greenberg, 2011; Bell and Hardingham, 2011), and are totally distinct from the toxic sequelae of excitotoxic Ca2+ influx (Hardingham and Bading, 2010; Wyllie et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hardingham and Bading, 2010; Wyllie et al., 2013.

claim: Activity-dependent gene expression programs direct neuroprotection in developing rodent neurons.
source: For example, rodent studies have shown that activity-dependent gene expression programs direct myriad processes in developing neurons, including neuroprotection, dendritic arborization, and synaptic plasticity (Konur and Ghosh, 2005; West and Greenberg, 2011; Bell and Hardingham, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Konur and Ghosh, 2005; West and Greenberg, 2011; Bell and Hardingham, 2011.

claim: Activity-dependent gene expression programs direct dendritic arborization in developing rodent neurons.
source: For example, rodent studies have shown that activity-dependent gene expression programs direct myriad processes in developing neurons, including neuroprotection, dendritic arborization, and synaptic plasticity (Konur and Ghosh, 2005; West and Greenberg, 2011; Bell and Hardingham, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Konur and Ghosh, 2005; West and Greenberg, 2011; Bell and Hardingham, 2011.

claim: Activity-dependent gene expression programs direct synaptic plasticity in developing rodent neurons.
source: For example, rodent studies have shown that activity-dependent gene expression programs direct myriad processes in developing neurons, including neuroprotection, dendritic arborization, and synaptic plasticity (Konur and Ghosh, 2005; West and Greenberg, 2011; Bell and Hardingham, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Konur and Ghosh, 2005; West and Greenberg, 2011; Bell and Hardingham, 2011.

claim: Certain neurodevelopmental disorders are associated with defects in activity-dependent transcriptional mechanisms.
source: Moreover, certain neurodevelopmental disorders are associated with defects in activity-dependent transcriptional mechanisms (West and Greenberg, 2011), making it important to fully understand transcriptional programs that are triggered by electrical activity in developing human neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to West and Greenberg, 2011.

claim: hESCCORT-neurons have sufficient homogeneity and electrical maturity to enable the study of activity-dependent gene expression.
source: Embryonic stem cell (ESC)-based technology enables the generation of glutamatergic cortical-patterned neurons from human embryonic stem cells (hESCCORT-neurons) of sufficient homogeneity and electrical maturity (Bilican et al., 2014; Livesey et al., 2014) to enable the study of activity-dependent gene expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bilican et al., 2014; Livesey et al., 2014.

claim: The Tc1 mouse carries a freely segregating copy of human chromosome-21.
source: Moreover, it is in theory possible to study mouse-human ortholog regulation in the same neuron by exploiting the aneuploid Tc1 mouse which carries a freely segregating copy of human chromosome-21, to identify whether any differences are independent of cellular environment (i.e. are due to DNA sequence divergence).
evidence: The claim is stated as a known fact about the Tc1 mouse model.

claim: Classical human stem cell-derived neurosphere-based preparations have a poor dynamic range in terms of gene regulation compared to primary mouse neuronal preparations.
source: These cells have a combination of homogeneity and electrical maturity that is hard to achieve with classical human stem cell-derived neurosphere-based preparations, which have a poor dynamic range in terms of gene regulation (Paşca et al., 2011) compared to primary mouse neuronal preparations (Spiegel et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Paşca et al., 2011 and Spiegel et al., 2014.

claim: L-type Ca2+ channel activation is an important mediator of activity-dependent gene regulation.
source: We studied transcriptional responses to L-type Ca2+ channel activation, an important mediator of activity-dependent gene regulation (West and Greenberg, 2011; Sheng et al., 1990; Bito et al., 1997; Deisseroth et al., 2003; Wheeler et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to West and Greenberg, 2011; Sheng et al., 1990; Bito et al., 1997; Deisseroth et al., 2003; Wheeler et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2014.

claim: KCl/FPL treatment leads to robust and uniform Ca2+ responses in hESCCORT-neurons.
source: To do this, hESCCORT-neurons were subject to KCl-induced membrane depolarization in the presence of the L-type Ca2+ channel agonist FPL64176 (KCl/FPL), which leads to robust and uniform Ca2+ responses ([Bilican et al., 2014], Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, Figure 1—source data 1) similar to rodent neurons (Hardingham et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bilican et al., 2014 and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: KCl/FPL treatment in hESCCORT-neurons produces Ca2+ responses similar to rodent neurons.
source: To do this, hESCCORT-neurons were subject to KCl-induced membrane depolarization in the presence of the L-type Ca2+ channel agonist FPL64176 (KCl/FPL), which leads to robust and uniform Ca2+ responses ([Bilican et al., 2014], Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, Figure 1—source data 1) similar to rodent neurons (Hardingham et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hardingham et al., 1999.

claim: KCl/FPL treatment robustly induces FOS in hESCCORT-neurons.
source: QPCR analysis revealed robust induction of classical early-response activity-regulated genes (ARGs) FOS, FOSL2 (FRA-2), and FOSB, and neurobiologically important ARGs BDNF, ARC, and NPAS4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b, Figure 1—source data 3) whose regulation has hitherto been studied primarily in rodent neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by QPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: KCl/FPL treatment robustly induces FOSL2 (FRA-2) in hESCCORT-neurons.
source: QPCR analysis revealed robust induction of classical early-response activity-regulated genes (ARGs) FOS, FOSL2 (FRA-2), and FOSB, and neurobiologically important ARGs BDNF, ARC, and NPAS4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b, Figure 1—source data 3) whose regulation has hitherto been studied primarily in rodent neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by QPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

evidence: The claim is supported by QPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The regulation of FOS, FOSL2, FOSB, BDNF, ARC, and NPAS4 has hitherto been studied primarily in rodent neurons.

evidence: The claim is stated as a fact about the historical focus of research on these genes.

claim: QPCR validation of fold-induction of selected ARGs revealed a tight correlation (r > 0.99) with the RNA-seq data in Hum-ESCCORT-neurons.
source: QPCR validation of fold-induction of selected ARGs revealed a tight correlation with the RNA-seq data (r > 0.99 for Hum-ESCCORT-neurons and mouse neurons respectively, Figure 1—figure supplement 1c, 1d, Figure 1—source data 4), supporting the reliability of the RNA-seq data set.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c, 1d.

claim: QPCR validation of fold-induction of selected ARGs revealed a tight correlation (r > 0.99) with the RNA-seq data in mouse neurons.
source: QPCR validation of fold-induction of selected ARGs revealed a tight correlation with the RNA-seq data (r > 0.99 for Hum-ESCCORT-neurons and mouse neurons respectively, Figure 1—figure supplement 1c, 1d, Figure 1—source data 4), supporting the reliability of the RNA-seq data set.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c, 1d.

claim: PER1 is induced >5-fold in both Hum-ESCCORT- and DIV10 Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons according to RNA-seq.
source: Genes induced >5-fold in both Hum-ESCCORT- and DIV10 Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons according to RNA-seq included neurobiologically important genes such as PER1, EGR2, EGR4 and ATF3 (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: EGR2 is induced >5-fold in both Hum-ESCCORT- and DIV10 Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons according to RNA-seq.
source: Genes induced >5-fold in both Hum-ESCCORT- and DIV10 Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons according to RNA-seq included neurobiologically important genes such as PER1, EGR2, EGR4 and ATF3 (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: EGR4 is induced >5-fold in both Hum-ESCCORT- and DIV10 Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons according to RNA-seq.
source: Genes induced >5-fold in both Hum-ESCCORT- and DIV10 Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons according to RNA-seq included neurobiologically important genes such as PER1, EGR2, EGR4 and ATF3 (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: ATF3 is induced >5-fold in both Hum-ESCCORT- and DIV10 Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons according to RNA-seq.
source: Genes induced >5-fold in both Hum-ESCCORT- and DIV10 Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons according to RNA-seq included neurobiologically important genes such as PER1, EGR2, EGR4 and ATF3 (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: There is a correlation (r = 0.480, p<0.0001) between Log2 (gene fold-change) in orthologous pairs between Hum-ESCCORT-neurons and DIV10 Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons.
source: Global comparison of Log2 (gene fold-change) in orthologous pairs revealed a correlation between Hum-ESCCORT-neurons and DIV10 Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons (r = 0.480, 95% CI: 0.465 to 0.494, p<0.0001, Figure 1d, Figure 1—source data 1), pointing to a significant, but incomplete, degree of conservation.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The correlation between activity-dependent gene fold-change in Hum-ESCCORT-neurons and DIV10 Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons points to a significant, but incomplete, degree of conservation.
source: Global comparison of Log2 (gene fold-change) in orthologous pairs revealed a correlation between Hum-ESCCORT-neurons and DIV10 Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons (r = 0.480, 95% CI: 0.465 to 0.494, p<0.0001, Figure 1d, Figure 1—source data 1), pointing to a significant, but incomplete, degree of conservation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the correlation coefficient (r = 0.480) observed in the data.

claim: The Log2 of the DRIs for 11,302 ortholog pairs are normally distributed about zero with a standard deviation of 0.68.
source: For the 11,302 ortholog pairs, we calculated the 'differential regulation index' (DRI), defined as the fold-change (Hum-ESCCORT-neurons) divided by the fold-change (Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons). The Log2 of the DRIs are normally distributed about zero with a standard deviation of 0.68 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e, Figure 1—source data 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by the distribution shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.

claim: There is a strong correlation (r = 0.834, p<0.0001) between KCl/FPL-induced gene regulation in DIV10 Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons and DIV4 Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons.
source: To address (i) we compared KCl/FPL-induced gene regulation in DIV10 Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons with that in synaptically immature DIV4 Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons, which revealed a strong correlation (p<0.0001, r = 0.834, 95% CI: 0.833 to 0.844, Figure 1e, Figure 1—source data 1), and a log2 DRI (DIV4:DIV10) distribution curve (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f, Figure 1—source data 5) substantially narrower than that observed in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Developmental stage does not have a large effect on the activity-responsiveness of genes at the 4h timepoint.
source: Taken together, this suggests that developmental stage does not have a large effect on the activity-responsiveness of genes at this time point and is unlikely to account for the human-mouse differences observed in Figure 1d.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the strong correlation (r = 0.834) between DIV4 and DIV10 mouse neurons and the narrower DRI distribution compared to human-mouse comparisons.

claim: Developmental stage is unlikely to account for the human-mouse differences in activity-dependent gene responsiveness observed.
source: Taken together, this suggests that developmental stage does not have a large effect on the activity-responsiveness of genes at this time point and is unlikely to account for the human-mouse differences observed in Figure 1d.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of developmental stage effects versus species effects on gene responsiveness.

claim: Mus-ESCCORT-neurons exhibit spontaneous firing.
source: To address (ii) (i.e. whether stem cell- vs. primary tissue origin causes differential gene responsiveness) we generated cortical-patterned neurons from mouse embryonic stem cells (Mus-ESCCORT-neurons) using established protocols (Gaspard et al., 2008), which exhibit spontaneous firing and synaptic activity (Figure 2a–d), similar to our Hum-ESCCORT-neurons (Bilican et al., 2014; Livesey et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2a–d.

claim: Mus-ESCCORT-neurons exhibit synaptic activity.
source: To address (ii) (i.e. whether stem cell- vs. primary tissue origin causes differential gene responsiveness) we generated cortical-patterned neurons from mouse embryonic stem cells (Mus-ESCCORT-neurons) using established protocols (Gaspard et al., 2008), which exhibit spontaneous firing and synaptic activity (Figure 2a–d), similar to our Hum-ESCCORT-neurons (Bilican et al., 2014; Livesey et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2a–d.

claim: Mus-ESCCORT-neurons exhibit spontaneous firing and synaptic activity similar to Hum-ESCCORT-neurons.
source: To address (ii) (i.e. whether stem cell- vs. primary tissue origin causes differential gene responsiveness) we generated cortical-patterned neurons from mouse embryonic stem cells (Mus-ESCCORT-neurons) using established protocols (Gaspard et al., 2008), which exhibit spontaneous firing and synaptic activity (Figure 2a–d), similar to our Hum-ESCCORT-neurons (Bilican et al., 2014; Livesey et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of electrophysiological data in Figure 2a–d and citations to Bilican et al., 2014; Livesey et al., 2014.

claim: There is a strong correlation (r = 0.748, p<0.0001) in gene-responsiveness between Mus-ESCCORT-neurons and DIV10 Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons.
source: A strong correlation was observed in gene-responsiveness in Mus-ESCCORT-neurons vs. Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons at either DIV10 or DIV4 (p<0.0001, r = 0.748 (DIV10), Figure 2e; r = 0.788, (DIV4), Figure 2f), significantly stronger than between Mus-ESCCORT- and Hum-ESCCORT-neurons (r = 0.596, Figure 2g, see also Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2e.

claim: There is a strong correlation (r = 0.788, p<0.0001) in gene-responsiveness between Mus-ESCCORT-neurons and DIV4 Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons.
source: A strong correlation was observed in gene-responsiveness in Mus-ESCCORT-neurons vs. Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons at either DIV10 or DIV4 (p<0.0001, r = 0.748 (DIV10), Figure 2e; r = 0.788, (DIV4), Figure 2f), significantly stronger than between Mus-ESCCORT- and Hum-ESCCORT-neurons (r = 0.596, Figure 2g, see also Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The correlation in gene-responsiveness between Mus-ESCCORT-neurons and Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons (r = 0.748 for DIV10, r = 0.788 for DIV4) is significantly stronger than between Mus-ESCCORT- and Hum-ESCCORT-neurons (r = 0.596).
source: A strong correlation was observed in gene-responsiveness in Mus-ESCCORT-neurons vs. Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons at either DIV10 or DIV4 (p<0.0001, r = 0.748 (DIV10), Figure 2e; r = 0.788, (DIV4), Figure 2f), significantly stronger than between Mus-ESCCORT- and Hum-ESCCORT-neurons (r = 0.596, Figure 2g, see also Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of correlation coefficients from Figures 2e, 2f, and 2g.

claim: All mouse neuronal preparations (primary DIV10, primary DIV4, and ESC-derived) correlated far more strongly with each other than with the human ESCCORT-neurons.
source: Indeed, a comparison of gene fold-change between all biological replicates in all data sets revealed that all mouse neuronal preparations (primary DIV10, primary DIV4, and ESC-derived) correlated far more strongly with each other than with the human ESCCORT-neurons. (Figure 2h).
evidence: The claim is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 2h.

claim: The weaker correlation with the hESCCORT-neurons may be due to some species-specific differences in neuronal gene activity-responsiveness, rather than differences in developmental stage or cellular origin.
source: This suggests that the weaker correlation with the hESCCORT-neurons may indeed be due to some species-specific differences in neuronal gene activity-responsiveness, rather than differences in developmental stage or cellular origin.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that mouse neurons of different developmental stages and origins cluster together, separate from human neurons.

claim: Basal neuronal gene expression shows less divergence than the responsiveness of genes to depolarization between human and mouse neurons.
source: Therefore basal neuronal gene expression shows less divergence than the responsiveness of genes to depolarization.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing correlation coefficients for basal expression (0.714, 0.711, 0.710) versus activity-dependent fold-change (0.480, 0.526, 0.595).

claim: There is no link between a gene's relative responsiveness to depolarization in human vs. mouse neurons, and its relative basal expression levels in human vs. mouse neurons.
source: As can be seen, there is no link between a gene's relative responsiveness to depolarization in human vs. mouse neurons, and its relative basal expression levels in human vs. mouse neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e showing no correlation between Log2(DRI) and Log2(DBEI).

claim: Evolutionary differences in activity-dependent gene responsiveness are not substantially attributable to differences in basal expression.
source: Thus, evolutionary differences in activity-dependent gene responsiveness are not substantially attributable to differences in basal expression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of correlation between DRI and DBEI.

claim: The Tc1 transchromosomic mouse strain carries a copy of human chromosome 21 (Hsa21) with approximately 10% deleted.
source: To investigate whether genetic sequence could be sufficient to quantitatively influence species-specific gene inducibility, we utilized neurons cultured from the Tc1 transchromosomic mouse strain which carries a copy of human chromosome 21 (Hsa21), albeit with approximately 10% deleted (O'Doherty et al., 2005; Gribble et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to O'Doherty et al., 2005; Gribble et al., 2013.

claim: The mouse genes in Tc1 neurons responded similarly to wild-type mouse neurons of the same age (r = 0.900).
source: We first verified that the mouse genes in Tc1 neurons responded similarly to wild-type mouse neurons of the same age (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a, Figure 3—source data 1, r = 0.900).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: There is a significant correlation (r = 0.730, p<0.0001) between Tc1 DRI and separate DRI for 72 orthologous pairs.
source: Importantly, we observed a significant correlation between these DRIs (p<0.0001, r = 0.730, Figure 3b, Figure 3—source data 2), meaning that differences in gene regulation observed in separate human and mouse cortical neuron preparations ('separate DRI') are broadly recapitulated when the orthologs are studied side-by-side in the same cellular environment ('Tc1 DRI').
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Differences in gene regulation observed in separate human and mouse cortical neuron preparations are broadly recapitulated when the orthologs are studied side-by-side in the same cellular environment.
source: Importantly, we observed a significant correlation between these DRIs (p<0.0001, r = 0.730, Figure 3b, Figure 3—source data 2), meaning that differences in gene regulation observed in separate human and mouse cortical neuron preparations ('separate DRI') are broadly recapitulated when the orthologs are studied side-by-side in the same cellular environment ('Tc1 DRI').
evidence: The claim is inferred from the significant correlation (r = 0.730) between Tc1 DRI and separate DRI.

claim: DNA sequence is a contributor to quantitative species-specific gene responsiveness.
source: This points to the DNA sequence as a contributor to quantitative species-specific gene responsiveness.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the recapitulation of species-specific differences in the Tc1 mouse model where human and mouse genes are in the same cellular environment.

claim: The human ETS2 ortholog is induced more strongly than the mouse ortholog in Tc1 neurons.
source: An example of such a gene is ETS2, the human ortholog of which is induced more strongly and rapidly than the mouse ortholog (Figure 3c,d, Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3c,d.

claim: The human ETS2 ortholog is induced more rapidly than the mouse ortholog.
source: An example of such a gene is ETS2, the human ortholog of which is induced more strongly and rapidly than the mouse ortholog (Figure 3c,d, Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3c,d.

claim: A region of the human ETS2 proximal promoter contains three human-specific AP-1 sites.
source: Interestingly, a region of its proximal promoter contains three human-specific AP-1 sites (Figure 3e, right) and was found to confer activity inducibility on a luciferase reporter, unlike the corresponding region of the mouse Ets2 promoter (Figure 3e, left).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis and reporter assay data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The human ETS2 proximal promoter region confers activity inducibility on a luciferase reporter.
source: Interestingly, a region of its proximal promoter contains three human-specific AP-1 sites (Figure 3e, right) and was found to confer activity inducibility on a luciferase reporter, unlike the corresponding region of the mouse Ets2 promoter (Figure 3e, left).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The corresponding region of the mouse Ets2 promoter does not confer activity inducibility on a luciferase reporter.
source: Interestingly, a region of its proximal promoter contains three human-specific AP-1 sites (Figure 3e, right) and was found to confer activity inducibility on a luciferase reporter, unlike the corresponding region of the mouse Ets2 promoter (Figure 3e, left).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Expression of inhibitory AP-1 mutant TAM67 inhibited Hum-ETS2-luciferase reporter induction.
source: Moreover, expression of inhibitory AP-1 mutant TAM67 (Brown et al., 1993) inhibited Hum-ETS2-luciferase reporter induction, and mutation of the three AP-1 sites to the corresponding mouse sequence abolished inducibility (Figure 3e).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Mutation of the three AP-1 sites in the human ETS2 promoter to the corresponding mouse sequence abolished inducibility.
source: Moreover, expression of inhibitory AP-1 mutant TAM67 (Brown et al., 1993) inhibited Hum-ETS2-luciferase reporter induction, and mutation of the three AP-1 sites to the corresponding mouse sequence abolished inducibility (Figure 3e).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The ETS2 proximal promoter contains functional human-specific AP-1 sites.
source: Thus, the ETS2 proximal promoter contains functional human-specific AP-1 sites, potentially contributing to the stronger and more rapid induction of the human ortholog in neurons
evidence: The claim is inferred from the reporter assay data showing that the human-specific AP-1 sites are necessary for activity-dependent induction.

claim: The functional human-specific AP-1 sites in the ETS2 promoter potentially contribute to the stronger and more rapid induction of the human ortholog in neurons.
source: Thus, the ETS2 proximal promoter contains functional human-specific AP-1 sites, potentially contributing to the stronger and more rapid induction of the human ortholog in neurons
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the functional data showing the AP-1 sites are necessary for induction.

claim: Of the top 100 most strongly induced human genes in Hum-ESCCORT-neurons (FC>3.5-fold, Padj<0.05), 85 are also induced in Mus-ESCCORT-neurons (FC>1.5-fold, Padj<0.05).
source: For example, of the top 100 most strongly induced human genes in Hum-ESCCORT-neurons (FC>3.5-fold, Padj<0.05), 85 are also induced in Mus-ESCCORT-neurons (FC>1.5-fold, Padj<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of RNA-seq data comparing human and mouse neurons.

claim: Of the top 100 most strongly induced human genes in Hum-ESCCORT-neurons, 91 are induced in at least one mouse neuronal preparation.
source: Of the remaining 15 genes, 6 are induced in DIV4 and/or DIV10 Mus-PRIMCORT-neurons, taking the total to 91/100.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of RNA-seq data across multiple mouse neuronal preparations.

claim: 409 out of 475 genes induced >2-fold (Padj<0.05) in Hum-ESCCORT-neurons are also induced (FC>1.5-fold, Padj<0.05) in one or more of the mouse neuronal preparations.
source: Conserved inducibility remains high even at a lower fold-change cut-off: e.g. 409 out of 475 genes induced >2-fold (Padj<0.05) in Hum-ESCCORT-neurons are also induced (FC>1.5-fold, Padj<0.05) in one or more of the mouse neuronal preparations.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of RNA-seq data across human and mouse neuronal preparations.

claim: Qualitative gene up/down regulation is well conserved between human and mouse neurons.
source: Although the focus of this study is understanding the extent and causes of differences in gene activity-responsiveness in human vs. mouse neurons, it should be noted that qualitative gene up/down regulation is well conserved.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the high proportion of genes showing conserved induction patterns across species.

claim: The study points to quantitative differences in activity-dependent gene-responsiveness in developing human neurons, compared to their mouse counterpart.
source: Nevertheless, our study points to quantitative differences in activity-dependent gene-responsiveness in developing human neurons, compared to their mouse counterpart, mediated at least in part by DNA sequence divergence.
evidence: The claim is supported by the overall findings of the study including correlation analyses and Tc1 mouse experiments.

claim: Quantitative differences in activity-dependent gene-responsiveness between human and mouse neurons are mediated at least in part by DNA sequence divergence.

source: More generally, given that diverse signal dependent transcriptional programs mediate cellular responses to physiological stimuli, as well as the effects (and side-effects) of pharmaceutical agents (Bell and Hardingham, 2011; Gupta et al., 2012; Bell et al., 2011; Hardingham and Lipton, 2011; Baxter et al., 2011), this study points to the value of employing human neurons as a tool to help bridge the translational gap between rodent studies, and human neurophysiology.
